system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-08-05 12:56:00 to 2134-08-07 15:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes presented with acute substernal chest pain, bradycardia, and nausea after a shower. He was found to have severe hyperkalemia (K+ 6.7) with ECG changes including peaked T waves and first-degree AV block. He received emergency treatment with calcium gluconate, insulin, dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, and Kayexalate, followed by emergent hemodialysis. His potassium normalized, chest pain resolved, and ECG returned to baseline. Serial troponins were stable, indicating no acute myocardial infarction. He remained hemodynamically stable on telemetry, completed a scheduled dialysis session, and was discharged home in good condition with medication adjustments and dietary instructions to avoid high-potassium foods.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Other diseases of trachea and bronchus
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you had chest pain earlier today and were brought in by EMS. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m feeling better now. The chest pain is gone, but I’m still a bit tired and worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We ran some tests in the ER, and your potassium level was very high—7.1, which can cause chest pain and heart rhythm issues. You were given calcium and other medications, then dialysis to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I just had this a few weeks ago. I didn’t eat anything different—just mushrooms and rice yesterday. I only eat one meal a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s important. Since you’re on dialysis, your body can’t remove potassium well. Even small amounts in food can build up. But since you’re denying dietary slip-up, we need to look at other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just me doing something wrong? I’ve been trying so hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes, even with good diet, potassium can rise due to how your kidneys work. We’ve consulted nephrology. They’ll look into whether you might have a hormonal issue like hypoaldosteronism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel a little better. But why the chest pain? Is my heart okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. High potassium can cause chest pain that mimics a heart attack. But your EKG showed peaked T waves—typical for hyperkalemia—and your troponin levels are stable, which means no heart muscle damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t a heart attack? That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like one. You also had a chest X-ray. It shows an enlarged heart, which we knew about, and a stable small fluid collection on the right side. Nothing new or dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart surgery before—CABG. But I get nervous when the pain comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. Given your history, we take chest pain very seriously. But this episode seems tied to your potassium. You’ve already had one dialysis session, and we’ll do another tomorrow to keep things stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on M-W-F dialysis this week instead of T-Th-Sat. Could that affect it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that could play a role. Longer gaps between sessions let potassium build up more. We’ll discuss with your dialysis team whether adjustments are needed long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They removed 2 liters today. I feel lighter already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That helps with fluid and potassium. We’ll monitor your levels closely. Your latest potassium after dialysis was 5.5—still a bit high but much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your labs from this morning. Your potassium is now 3.7, which is in the safe range. Creatinine dropped to 6.6, so dialysis is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I haven’t had any chest pain since yesterday. I walked to the bathroom without getting short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s a great sign. Your hemoglobin did drop a bit—from 11.7 to 10.1. But it’s likely due to fluid shifts after dialysis, not bleeding. Your stool test was negative, so no internal bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Procrit for anemia. Should that be adjusted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your team is managing that. No change needed now. We’ll keep monitoring. You’ll have another dialysis session today, then we’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need any new medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Nephrology is considering prescribing Kayexalate on non-dialysis days to help remove extra potassium. But that’s still being discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember taking that before. It’s not the most pleasant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll only use it if necessary. For now, nutrition will come by to review low-potassium food choices—even healthy foods like mushrooms can be high in potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had no idea mushrooms were high. I thought I was eating safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not always obvious. A dietitian will help you identify hidden sources. Even one meal can make a difference when your kidneys aren’t working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just finished your second dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but okay. No pain, no dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable. Labs show potassium at 3.7, which is ideal. We’re confident you’re improving. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my meds? Anything changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a few updates. Your lisinopril dose is being increased from 2.5 mg to 5 mg daily. It helps your heart and blood pressure, and we’ll monitor your potassium closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Is it safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at this low dose. It actually protects your kidneys in diabetes. We’ll keep checking your levels. Also, you’re now prescribed docusate for constipation, which can affect potassium too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And sevelamer—still with meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sevelamer carbonate now—same dose, with every meal. It binds phosphorus and helps control potassium indirectly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’ve cleared you for discharge. You have a follow-up with Dr. Patel at 10:50 a.m. today—same day, great timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make it. So, no chest pain, potassium is down, and I’m safe to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your chest pain was due to high potassium, not a heart attack. You had two dialysis sessions, and your labs are stable. Keep taking your meds, follow the low-potassium diet, and call if you feel chest pain, dizziness, or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything. I feel much more in control now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay consistent with dialysis, watch your diet, and we’ll get to the bottom of why your potassium keeps rising. You’re doing the right things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll see you or my nephrologist soon. Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Go home safely and rest.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for left-sided chest pain associated with severe hyperkalemia (potassium 7.1) and EKG changes. He received emergency treatment with calcium gluconate and underwent emergent hemodialysis, which improved his symptoms and normalized potassium. Serial troponins were stable, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. He remained chest pain-free, completed a second dialysis session, and was discharged home in stable condition. The rise in potassium was not clearly due to dietary indiscretion; nephrology will evaluate for underlying causes such as hypoaldosteronism. Medications were adjusted, including increasing lisinopril and adding docusate, and low-potassium diet counseling was provided.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
